summary: This note is a collection of Wikipedia-derived passages about Tucson, Arizona. It covers the city's water conservation and groundwater efforts using CAP water, its desert climate and weather records at the University of Arizona and the airport, and its population, demographics and metropolitan size. It also describes local culture and infrastructure, including cycling routes, television stations, city council elections, historic horse and auto racetracks, and the 'A' Mountain landmark on Sentinel Peak.
one_line: Overview of Tucson, Arizona covering water policy, desert climate, population, cycling, media, elections, racetracks and Sentinel Peak.
key_facts: Tucson's Central Arizona Project (CAP) allocation annually provides over 20 million gallons of recharged water, and since 2001 CAP water has allowed the city to remove or turn off over 80 wells.
The Central Arizona Project Aqueduct passes more than 300 mi (480 km) across the desert from the Colorado River.
The 2010 United States Census put Tucson's city population at 520,116 and the metropolitan area population at 980,263.
Tucson is located 118 mi (190 km) southeast of Phoenix in one passage and 108 miles (174 km) southeast of Phoenix in another, and 60 mi (97 km) north of the U.S.-Mexico border.
Tucson is the largest city in southern Arizona and the second largest in the state after Phoenix.
Roughly 150 Tucson companies are involved in the design and manufacture of optics and optoelectronics systems, earning Tucson the nickname Optics Valley.
The record maximum temperature at the University of Arizona was 115 °F (46 °C) on June 19, 1960, and July 28, 1995; the record minimum was 6 °F (−14 °C) on January 7, 1913.
Tucson averages 11.8 inches (299.7 mm) of precipitation per year and has a desert climate (Köppen BWh) due to its high evapotranspiration.
Tucson was awarded a gold rating for bicycle-friendliness by the League of American Bicyclists in 2006.
The Loop is a network of seven linear parks comprising over 100 mi (160 km) of paved, vehicle-free trails that encircles the majority of the city.
Tucson is the 68th largest designated market area in the U.S. with 433,310 homes, limited to the three counties of southeastern Arizona (Pima, Santa Cruz, and Cochise).
Both the council members and the mayor serve four-year terms, and none face term limits.
Rillito Downs held the first organized quarter horse races in the world, and it still hosts racing.
The most recent snowfall was on February 20, 2013, when 2.0 inches of snow blanketed the city, the largest since 1987.
Anti-war activists painted the 'A' on Sentinel Peak black at the beginning of the Iraq War; it is now red, white and blue except when a biennial election chooses another color.
